questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A promise the course cannot keep
questions.learningObjective: identify who a syllabus over-promise disadvantages most
questions.stem: A syllabus promises that each week's assigned reading will be discussed in depth, while setting twenty pages a week for a group large enough that discussion time is scarce. Who does the promise fall hardest on?

options.text: Students who prepare carefully and reach the hour able to raise only the first few pages of the week's reading
Students who do not prepare, since a promise about discussion affects them least when they attend to listen
options.misconception: assumes the unprepared are spared, when the promise is what makes their silence read as a choice

options.text: The teaching staff, since the promise obliges them to cover a depth that no seminar hour could ever reach
options.misconception: puts the cost on the people delivering the promise rather than on those who rely on it

options.text: Nobody, since promising discussion is a way of encouraging preparation rather than a claim about coverage
options.misconception: reads a promise as a motivational device and so treats it as making no commitment at all

questions.explanation: An unkeepable promise is not harmless, because a student who has done the work the promise asked for discovers that the work could not be used, and the discovery falls hardest on the students with the most preparation behind them. The first option identifies that group. The second assumes the unprepared are spared when the promise is exactly what makes their silence a judgement, the third puts the cost on the staff who made the promise, and the fourth insists a promise is only encouragement and so commits nobody to anything.
questions.hint: Ask who is most exposed when a stated expectation is not met in practice.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Where an over-promise lands unevenly
questions.learningObjective: trace how a course promise falls hardest on the students least able to meet it
questions.stem: A syllabus says that credit depends on having read the assigned material closely, and that discussion of un-read material counts for little. All coursework is set at the end of term. What follows from that arrangement?

options.text: Students who fell behind early have least time to catch up, so the promise weighs on them most heavily for the shortfall
Nothing unfair follows, since every student has the same total time to read the same amount of material
options.misconception: counts total time available and ignores that the material piled up earlier leaves more of it unread

options.text: The arrangement rewards thorough readers, since end-of-term coursework gives anyone behind more time to prepare
options.misconception: reads a deadline as extra preparation time and misses that it compresses the catch-up period

options.text: Nothing follows either way, since no marker could tell which of the assigned pages any student had read
options.misconception: argues from marker inability and leaves the incentive the promise itself creates

questions.explanation: A promise about reading plus a single deadline produces a running deficit for anyone who falls behind, because each week's shortfall joins the next week's load, and by the end of term the students who are worst prepared are the ones with the least time in which to recover. The first option says this. The second counts hours available rather than hours of unread material outstanding, the third mistakes a deadline for a gift of time, and the fourth defends the arrangement on grounds of what markers can detect rather than what it asks of students.
questions.hint: Follow the arithmetic: what happens to a student's backlog each week they do not catch up?

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An unread reading load and the writing that suffers
questions.learningObjective: explain why an unread reading load degrades the writing produced from it
questions.stem: A reading list sets forty pages a week for a seminar that needs about one page. Students skim, and the reading responses come out thinner than in earlier terms. What accounts for the thinning?

options.text: The responses were built on skimmed pages, so there is less in them to react to and the argument has nothing to hold on to
The responses are thinner because students have less time overall, and the length of the list is beside the point
options.misconception: locates the cause in a general shortage of time and lets the reading load go unchecked

options.text: The responses are thinner because the assignment now asks for less than the same assignment asked for before
options.misconception: attributes the change to the task and ignores that the material behind it also changed

options.text: The responses are thinner because seminar groups reward short writing, and the writing follows the group's preference
options.misconception: explains a writing change by a preference and leaves the reading behind the writing unexamined

questions.explanation: Writing about a text is a reaction to what is in it, so when a list guarantees that the text was skimmed, the response has correspondingly less to work with and the argument cannot get past restatement. The first option puts the cause where it belongs, in the relationship between what was read and what was written. The second invokes a general shortage of time, the third blames the task rather than its material, and the fourth treats a preference of the group as a cause when the group's reading is the thing that changed.
questions.hint: Ask what the skimming left in the pages for a response to work on.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Preparation that no one can verify
questions.learningObjective: identify what a written submission becomes when it is drafted from an unread reading
questions.stem: A group sets a long reading for one week. Two members read it fully; two skim it. One member drafts the whole written response in a single sitting without circulating it. What is the group most likely to have?

options.text: One member's reading of the text, presented as the group's, and none of the two full readers' objections anywhere in it
A response giving all four positions equal space, so every member's reading is represented in the finished page
options.misconception: assumes an undrafted response distributes weight evenly among members who read differently

options.text: A shorter response than usual, since work written in one sitting cannot be as long as a response drafted together
options.misconception: predicts a length difference and leaves the single reader's unrepresented views untouched

options.text: A more accurate response, since one member's full reading is a sounder basis than four partial ones
options.misconception: treats majority coverage as a fault and rewards a single account as more reliable

questions.explanation: When one person writes from their own reading and nobody circulates a draft, the two members who read the text properly have no way to register what they found, so the response carries a single account of a contested reading and presents it as though it were shared. The first option is that outcome. The second assumes averaging happens without any mechanism for it, the third predicts only a length change, and the fourth commits the error this subject exists to catch, treating one voice as more reliable because the others were quieter.
questions.hint: Ask which members' reading of the text appears in the finished response, and which does not.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A norm nobody enforces
questions.learningObjective: trace what a discussion norm becomes when no one is given the job of enforcing it
questions.stem: A seminar agrees that nobody speaks for a full minute without a signal that others want to hear more. No one is given the job of watching for it. What typically follows?

options.text: The longest speakers keep going, because a norm nobody watches is read as permission by the people it constrains
The norm holds, since members who care about it will interrupt on their own account when a turn runs long
options.misconception: relies on goodwill alone and ignores how a norm with no cost is read by others

options.text: The norm is struck from the group's charter at the next meeting, since it was never being observed
options.misconception: supposes a formal removal when what happens is a silent failure to apply the norm

options.text: The group splits into enforcers and members who refuse any enforcement, and the limit becomes a matter of factions
options.misconception: predicts a durable split where the likelier outcome is no enforcement at all

questions.explanation: Norms are read as permissions when nothing happens the first time they are broken, and the people bound by a norm are exactly the ones who read it correctly in the absence of any consequence, so the longest turns tend to stay longest. The first option says this. The second relies on members volunteering to enforce a limit over themselves, the third imagines a formal removal where the ordinary outcome is that the norm simply stops applying, and the fourth predicts a durable faction fight that this kind of failure does not usually produce.
questions.hint: Ask what a member concludes from the first time the limit is passed without any reaction.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Making a norm enforceable
questions.learningObjective: choose the pair of arrangements most likely to hold a norm without anybody policing it
questions.stem: A seminar's hour-long time limit keeps failing. Which pair of arrangements is most likely to hold it without anybody policing it?

options.text: The group takes the first turn each week and the limit is written into the closing statement, so both ends of the hour are already spoken for
The limit is settled once at the start of term and then left to the members, so the group's attention can return to the readings
options.misconception: treats agreement as the enforcement mechanism when only attention enforces anything

options.text: The limit applies only to whoever is facilitating, who is the member best placed to end a turn without offence
options.misconception: confines the limit to one role and leaves every other long turn unconstrained

options.text: The limit is announced in the handbook rather than agreed in the room, so it binds without anyone feeling it was imposed
options.misconception: believes anonymity produces compliance and overlooks what a publicly agreed limit does

questions.explanation: A limit holds when the group's own routine fills the space that the limit is protecting, so a first turn that always closes on time and a closing statement that everyone expects to read together both put the boundary inside the ordinary sequence of the hour rather than inside a person's restraint. The first pair does that. The second replaces enforcement with agreement, the third restricts the limit to the person least able to enforce it against peers, and the fourth believes that a rule announced from outside binds more firmly than one the group adopted itself.
questions.hint: Ask which arrangements put the limit inside the group's routine rather than inside a member's willpower.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A question too broad to answer
questions.learningObjective: explain what happens to discussion when a question covers a whole field
questions.stem: A week's discussion question asks what we ought to think about expertise. The hour fills with anecdotes and the group agrees nothing at the end. Why did the question fail?

options.text: It names no particular claim for anyone to accept or resist, so replies can only describe preferences rather than test each other
It is too specific, since it turns on a single concept and leaves members no room to bring their own cases
options.misconception: reverses the fault, since a question this broad is wide rather than narrow

options.text: It asks a question of fact, and the group had not done the reading needed to answer questions of fact
options.misconception: supplies a remedy that would not help, since the difficulty is what kind of answer is possible

options.text: It asks a question of value, and this course does not permit members to disagree about values
options.misconception: invents a course rule and leaves the question's shape untouched

questions.explanation: A discussion question earns its place by naming something a member could answer differently, and a question about what we ought to think about expertise offers no claim to hold and no consequence to fear, so the only available moves are illustrations and the group ends where anecdotes always end. The first option explains that. The second reverses the fault, the third proposes more reading where the problem is that no reading would produce an answer of the kind asked for, and the fourth invents a restriction on the course that the account nowhere suggests.
questions.hint: Ask what a member would have to assert for the question to be answered.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A question that supplies its own answer
questions.learningObjective: identify the working assumption a discussion question smuggles into the room
questions.stem: A discussion question asks how the new reading list improved preparation. Most members report that they now prepare more, and the hour is spent on which changes worked best. What has the question settled?

options.text: That preparation improved, so the group's replies are about how the improvement happened rather than whether it did
That the reading list is long, which members can confirm and are then free to discuss in any direction they like
options.misconception: reads the question as neutral and locates its assumption in a fact nobody needed to assume

options.text: That preparation is measured by pages read, which is a definition the question quietly settles for the group
options.misconception: identifies a real unstated definition and misses the larger claim the phrasing already granted

options.text: That the group reads slowly, which is what makes the effect on preparation hard to see in one term
options.misconception: supplies a trait for the members and leaves the assumption inside the question standing

questions.explanation: To ask how something improved is to grant that it improved, and once that is granted the group's remaining business is detail, so the discussion that looked open was in fact settled before the first member spoke. The first option says what was settled and what the replies therefore became. The second calls the question neutral, the third identifies a genuine unstated definition but treats it as the whole of the problem, and the fourth attributes a reading speed to the group and leaves the assumption in the question untouched.
questions.hint: Ask what the group would have had to do first if the improvement were in doubt.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An opening that closes a thread
questions.learningObjective: identify how an opening move signals that a line of reply is unwelcome
questions.stem: A member opens by saying the reading's theory is long discredited and that anyone still using it must have missed the recent literature. What happens to the thread about that theory?

options.text: Anyone wanting to raise the theory must now argue against the dismissal before the theory itself can be discussed
The thread strengthens, since the opening has given the group a clear current position to test and work from
options.misconception: reads a dismissal as a contribution and misses the barrier it puts in front of replies

options.text: The thread ends by agreement, since the opening settles a question the group had been circling for several weeks
options.misconception: assumes a dismissal carries the authority to settle anything without being argued

options.text: The thread turns to method, since attention naturally shifts from a claim to the way it was tested
options.misconception: predicts a shift of subject and leaves the effect of the dismissal on willing speakers unexamined

questions.explanation: Calling a theory discredited and blaming anyone who still uses it changes what a member has to do before they can speak, because the price of raising the theory has become a separate argument about the recent literature, and most members pay that price or drop the thread. The first option describes that. The second treats the dismissal as a gift of clarity, the third gives one member's opening the standing to close a question the group had not settled, and the fourth predicts a topic shift that leaves the effect on speakers unaccounted for.
questions.hint: Ask what a member has to settle before they can discuss the reading's theory at all.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Repairing an opening that shuts a thread
questions.learningObjective: choose the rewrite of an opening that leaves the thread available
questions.stem: A member opens a seminar by calling a reading's theory discredited and blaming anyone who still uses it. Which rewrite keeps the thread open without conceding anything?

options.text: The reading treats the theory as settled, which is worth pressing on, since it never sets out the case for doubting the theory
The theory is discredited, so the reading's method should be set aside with it, since a method cannot outlive its theory
options.misconception: accepts the dismissal and extends it, so the thread is closed rather than redirected

options.text: The reading is out of date on this point, so the group should consult more recent work before discussing the theory further
options.misconception: defers the discussion to a later date while treating the dismissal as established

options.text: The theory is still contested, so the group should treat the reading as one side of an argument that remains open
options.misconception: concedes a contestable point about the state of the literature in order to sound even-handed

questions.explanation: A rewrite keeps a thread alive by moving the pressure from the people who hold the position to the text itself, and the first version does that, since it turns a dismissal into a question about an omission in the reading that anyone may press. The second accepts the dismissal and extends it, the third postpones the discussion while treating the dismissal as fact, and the fourth is the subtlest failure because it makes a claim about the state of the literature in order to sound fair, conceding exactly the ground the opening was trying to take.
questions.hint: Ask which rewrite moves the challenge onto the reading rather than onto the people who disagree with it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What enforcing a norm requires
questions.learningObjective: name a norm's enforcement mechanism, then say what a group would accept to install it
questions.stem: A group cannot get its time limit to hold. First say what enforces a norm, then say what this group would have to give up. What should the first answer contain?

options.text: Something in the group's own routine that ends a turn on time without a person policing it
A member whose assigned job is to interrupt, since only another person can end a long turn
options.misconception: assumes enforcement must be a person and misses what the group's own sequence can do

options.text: A written rule in the group's charter, since an unwritten norm is the kind most often broken
options.misconception: makes writing the mechanism and passes over why unwritten rules often fail to bite

options.text: A discussion of the limit at the start of each meeting, so that everyone present has agreed to it
options.misconception: treats fresh agreement as enforcement and overlooks that agreements need a cost to hold

questions.explanation: A norm is enforced by something that happens whether or not anyone chooses to enforce it, and the first answer names that correctly by pointing at the group's own routine, which is the only place a limit can live if it is not going to depend on a member's willingness to interrupt a peer. The second makes enforcement a job, which works until the holder is tired or unwilling, the third assumes that writing a rule creates a cost, and the fourth confuses agreement with consequence.
questions.hint: Ask what would end a long turn if every member in the room were unwilling to interrupt.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a rotating role distributes
questions.learningObjective: state what a rotating facilitation role spreads across a group
questions.stem: A seminar rotates the note-taker and the timekeeper between members each week. What does the rotation distribute that a permanent holder would not?

options.text: The cost of watching the group instead of arguing in it, so no one member pays for everyone's process alone
The skill of note-taking, so that every member becomes equally able to summarise a discussion afterwards
options.misconception: claims a training benefit and misses what rotation is actually distributing

options.text: The authority to end a discussion, so that the group's decisions each week come from a different member
options.misconception: grants a decision-making power that a note-taker and timekeeper do not hold

options.text: The written record of the meeting, so that no member is left holding an account of what others said
options.misconception: treats rotation as protecting members from the record rather than sharing the group's work

questions.explanation: A facilitation role makes a member watch the group while not participating fully in it, which is a real cost, and rotation is the arrangement that spreads that cost rather than concentrating it on whoever volunteered first. The first option says this. The second describes a training benefit that rotation may incidentally produce, the third gives the role a decision-making authority that note-taking and time-keeping do not carry, and the fourth treats the record as a burden to be escaped rather than a piece of the group's work.
questions.hint: Ask what the holder of the role gives up, and who pays that when the role is permanent.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A rotation that does not reach everyone
questions.learningObjective: identify who a rotating role excludes in practice
questions.stem: A group rotates the timekeeper in the order members joined the course, weekly. Six weeks in, the member who joined last has held the role once, at the start. What does the record show?

options.text: The order of rotation is the order of joining, so the newest member is the one whose turn keeps arriving last
The rotation is working, since one turn in six weeks is a normal gap when a group has more members than slots
options.misconception: treats a schedule that never reaches someone as an ordinary outcome of rotation

options.text: The newest member is avoiding the role, since nobody had to ask them to take it more than once
options.misconception: assigns responsibility to a member for a schedule they did not set or control

options.text: The role matters so little that a six-week gap shows the group has decided it does not need the role at all
options.misconception: infers that the role is unimportant from who has not yet held it

questions.explanation: A rotation fixes a rule, and a rule that follows join order is a rule that reaches the newest member last every time, so the practice that is supposed to spread the group's work ends up practising it least where a member is newest and least secure. The first option names what the schedule is doing. The second calls the outcome normal, the third blames a member for a sequence they did not set, and the fourth draws a conclusion about the role's importance from a fact about who has held it.
questions.hint: Ask what the order of rotation is a function of, and where in that order each member sits.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A redirect that also silences
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an intervention that redirects a thread from one that ends it
questions.stem: A member interrupts to say the discussion has drifted from the reading and should return to it. The thread on the reading stops and does not return for a fortnight. What happened?

options.text: The group was moved without the speaker being carried along, so the thread was redirected out of existence
The intervention worked, since the group returned to the reading and the drift it complained of was corrected
options.misconception: accepts a complaint as evidence of an outcome and ignores the thread that did not return

options.text: The speaker was silenced but the thread survived and reappeared once the group came back to the reading
options.misconception: preserves a thread the record says did not return, and so credits the group with recovery

options.text: Speaker and thread were both served, since changing subject by interruption is the seminar's normal way of proceeding
options.misconception: normalises the effect and leaves the loss of the thread unexplained

questions.explanation: A redirect that stops a thread is not a redirect but a termination, and the test is whether the thread could have come back, which here it could not for a fortnight, so the speaker was not redirected along with the group. The first option says this. The second treats the intervention's own complaint as proof that it worked, the third asserts a recovery the record contradicts, and the fourth calls the loss of a thread normal without accounting for what was lost with it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the interrupted thread ever came back, and what that tells you about the interruption.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Analyzing a redirect
questions.learningObjective: say what an intervention redirected, then say what it needed to leave intact
questions.stem: A facilitator stops a thread on local pay, says the course holds no evidence about pay, and invites the group back to the reading. First say what the intervention redirected, then say what it should have preserved. What should the first answer contain?

options.text: The group was moved off a topic the course cannot support, which was right on its own terms and still left something unpaid for
The group was moved off a topic members had raised deliberately, which the intervention never acknowledged before ending it
options.misconception: confuses the reason the redirect was justified with the reason the thread died as it did

options.text: The facilitator substituted a topic of their own for one the group owned, which is what the role of facilitator permits
options.misconception: grants facilitators a licence to replace a group's thread and treats the loss as legitimate

options.text: The group was moved to ground the reading settles, since the reading is the only ground this course can defend
options.misconception: assumes the reading settles the pay question and so misses what was actually at issue

questions.explanation: The first answer separates two things the group needs to keep apart, namely that the facilitator was right that the course had no evidence about pay and that ending a thread members had raised deliberately still disposes of something the course had not settled. questions.hint: Keep the reason for the redirect separate from what the redirect actually did to the thread.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Consensus where the record shows a split
questions.learningObjective: identify what a claim of consensus conceals about the group's own record
questions.stem: A group's synthesis states that members agreed the reading was persuasive. The discussion record shows three members objecting to its central claim and none of them withdrawing. What has the synthesis reported?

options.text: Agreement the record does not contain, so the objections have vanished from the group's account of itself
Agreement, since members who object in the room often accept the outcome once it has been written down
options.misconception: assumes writing converts objection into assent and lets the record go unchecked

options.text: A decision, since a group that records a position is entitled to act on that position afterwards
options.misconception: treats a record of agreement as authorising action and sidesteps whether agreement existed

options.text: Disagreement, since the objections are in the record and a synthesis that mentions them is reporting a split
options.misconception: claims the synthesis reports a split when the words it uses report the opposite

questions.explanation: A synthesis is the group's only durable account of what it thought, so when it reports agreement that the record contradicts, the disagreement is not merely misdescribed but effectively removed from the record's future readers, who will have no way of knowing it existed. The first option says that. The second invents a conversion from objection to assent, the third treats the record as conferring authority rather than as making a claim that can be checked, and the fourth says the synthesis reports a split when its own words do the opposite.
questions.hint: Ask whether any member who objected ever said they had been persuaded.

questions.topic: Minutes that record agreement after a split exchange
questions.learningObjective: identify what a set of minutes converts when it smooths a divided discussion
questions.stem: In a recorded discussion two members disagree about whether the reading's evidence is strong, one of them twice. The minutes say the group explored the question and found the evidence compelling. What have the minutes done?

options.text: Turned a split into a finding, so a later reader of the record cannot see that anyone disagreed at all
Recorded the discussion accurately, since a minute is a summary and a summary selects what mattered
options.misconception: defends the minutes as summary and treats the disagreement as merely unselected detail

options.text: Preserved the disagreement, since it names the question that was examined and the positions taken on it
options.misconception: credits the minutes with a record of positions that the minutes' own wording denies

options.text: Settled the question deliberately, which is a legitimate way for a group to close a long discussion
options.misconception: credits a decision the minutes record no vote or agreement to support

questions.hint: Ask what a reader consulting only the minutes would conclude about whether the group was divided.

questions.topic: A synthesis that flattens what it reports
questions.learningObjective: explain why a written synthesis can report a disagreement badly
questions.stem: A synthesis of a week in which two positions were argued at length says the group discussed the question and identified several considerations bearing on it. What is lost?

options.text: Which considerations belonged to which position, so no reader can tell what anyone was arguing for or against
The length of the discussion, which a synthesis is not obliged to reproduce at the same length
options.misconception: identifies something a summary is not required to keep and passes over what it did keep

options.text: The reading itself, which the discussion was about and which a synthesis may reasonably take as given
options.misconception: names material a synthesis can omit and misses the part of the exchange that was actually lost

options.text: The names of the speakers, since a synthesis normally reports positions rather than attributing them

questions.topic: Keeping a disagreement visible in writing

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Why a seminar records what it decided against
questions.learningObjective: justify keeping a written record of the positions a group rejected
questions.stem: Explain why a seminar should keep a written record of the positions it decided against, and not only of the ones it adopted.

answer.exemplar: A record of what a group rejected is the only thing that makes the decision it adopted intelligible later, because a decision without its alternatives reads as arbitrary and a reader who was not in the room has no way of telling a considered choice from an accident of who spoke. The second reason concerns the members. A group that records only what it adopted gives its more persuasive members the impression that their view survived the discussion, while the members who were argued out of theirs find their reasoning absent from the group's account of itself, and the asymmetry is repeated every week until the people who lost an argument stop offering one. The third reason is that rejected positions are the ones a group most needs later, since when a question comes back, as questions in a course do, the arguments that failed are already written down and can be examined rather than reconstructed from memory by whoever remembers them most clearly. Keeping the rejected view is also what makes a synthesis honest, because a synthesis that reports only the surviving position is indistinguishable from one written by a group in which no disagreement ever happened.

questions.explanation: A strong response explains that a decision is unintelligible without its alternatives, that omitting rejected positions tells the members who lost an argument that their reasoning did not count, and that rejected arguments are what a group can reuse when the question returns.
questions.hint: Ask what a later reader cannot tell about a decision that is recorded without the alternatives.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Why an over-promising syllabus falls hardest on the prepared
questions.learningObjective: explain why an unkeepable course promise harms its most committed students most
questions.stem: Explain why a syllabus promise the course cannot keep does its greatest harm to the students who prepared most carefully.

answer.exemplar: The harm falls on the prepared students because the promise is a contract about what will be done with their work, and a student who read forty pages in order to have them discussed has made an investment that the course quietly declines to honour, while a student who read nothing loses nothing at all because the reading was never what the discussion was going to reward. The second reason is diagnostic. Once a promise has been broken repeatedly, the prepared learn that preparation does not predict what happens in the room, and that lesson generalises well beyond the one seminar, so the course teaches its members to withhold effort from anything it cannot guarantee. The third is that the damage is invisible from inside the course, since the staff delivered what the hour allowed and the students who withdrew quietly are not the ones who fill the evaluation forms. What makes this hard to correct is that the promise is usually made in good faith, by people who intend to keep it, and the students who are harmed by its failure are the ones least likely to complain, since complaining requires believing the course meant what it said.

questions.explanation: A strong response explains that the promise commits the course to use the prepared students' work and so breaks a contract with them alone, that members learn effort does not pay when a promise is broken, and that the resulting withdrawal is invisible to the staff who set the promise in good faith.
questions.hint: Ask who loses most when a promised discussion of their reading does not happen.
